issues.title: Total sketching-solver complexity

failure_location.quote: Specifically,~the~time~complexity can be reduced to $O(\texttt{nnz(S)}d)$, where $S\in\mR^{d\times q}$ is the sketching matrix with $q\ll d$. For instance, when $S$ is a sparse sketching vector, the time complexity is $O(d)$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The computational complexity includes $O(\tau\cdot\texttt{nnz(S)}d)$ flops for computing the sketched Newton direction and $O(d^2)$~flops for updating $\hat{\Xi}_t$.

For instance, when $S\sim \text{Unif}(\{\be_i\}_{i=1}^d)$, \cite{Na2022Statistical} showed~$\tau = O(d)$, suggesting that the overall computational complexity of sketched Newton inference~is $O(d^2)$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the sketching solver costs O(nnz(S)d), and O(d) for a sparse sketching vector. The old construction actually applies the update in sec2:equ2 τ times before nequ:8 defines the direction, while the later complexity discussion explicitly gives O(τ·nnz(S)d) and, when τ=O(d), O(d²). The advertised total cost therefore understates the work by a factor of τ.
issues.overall_effect: The introduction understates the solver's total computational cost and its dimension dependence, although the algorithm and formal convergence results are unchanged.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Distinguish the cost of one inner sketch update from the total solver cost: one update costs O(nnz(S)d), whereas computing the direction after τ updates costs O(τ·nnz(S)d). For a sparse sketching vector with τ=O(d), state the total solver cost as O(d²). No algorithmic or convergence result needs alteration.
issues.why_classification: The omitted factor τ is directly recoverable, but correcting it withdraws the coherent advertised O(d) total-complexity promise and worsens its dimension dependence to O(d²), so this is not a typo or same-guarantee minor repair. The correction is nevertheless local, leaves the method and proofs unchanged, and retains a recognizably comparable complexity advantage over an O(d³) exact solve; thus the loss is limited rather than major.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Specifically, the time complexity of solving the Newton system can be reduced to $O(\tau\cdot\texttt{nnz}(S)d)$, where $S\in\mR^{d\times q}$ is the sketching matrix with $q\ll d$; $\tau$ denotes the number of sketching steps; and $\texttt{nnz}(S)$ denotes the number of nonzero entries of $S$. For instance, when $S$ is a sparse sketching vector, one can have $\tau = O(d)$ and lead to the time complexity of $O(d^2)$.

issues.title: Higher-order adaptivity threshold

failure_location.quote: Similar to Lemma \ref{sec4:lem1}, $\chi\geq2\beta$ (i.e., $\chi_t\lesssim \beta_t^2$)~makes~the adaptivity error $\chi_t/\beta_t^{1.5}$ higher order.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that χ≥2β makes the adaptivity term higher order. The old theorem actually establishes a baseline √β_t for 0<β≤0.5 and 1/√(tβ_t) for β>0.5. At the admissible boundary χ=2β in the first regime, χ_t/β_t^{1.5}=Θ(√β_t), so it has the same order. Higher order requires χ>2β there; in the second regime the sharp comparison is χ>β+0.5.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem and consistency result remain valid, but the prose incorrectly tells readers that the boundary choice χ=2β makes adaptivity negligible in the lower-β regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the higher-order comparison by the regime-wise thresholds forced by Theorem sec4:thm1: require χ>2β when 0<β≤1/2 and χ>β+1/2 when 1/2<β<1. In particular, do not call χ=2β higher order in the lower-β regime. No theorem or proof needs modification.
issues.why_classification: The displayed rates and the stated power-law sequences uniquely force these strict comparisons. At χ=2β in the lower regime, the adaptivity term is Θ(√β_t), so the boundary cannot coherently satisfy the stated higher-order property. An adept reader can correct this comparison boundary directly from the old source without repairing any inference or construction.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: From the result, we see that if $\beta \in (0,0.5]$, then choosing $\chi > 2\beta$ (i.e., $\chi_t \lesssim \beta_t^2$) makes the adaptivity error term $\chi_t / \beta_t^{1.5}$ of higher order (although this case is less interesting, since existing normality analyses typically require $\beta > 0.5$).
